sentences.text: In Part One, we separated a written claim, its proof, and the meaning of its symbols.
Now we return to a calculation we can actually inspect.
One third is an exact number… but a decimal display has room for only finitely many digits.
If we stop at zero point three three three… we have changed the number.
Multiply that displayed decimal by three, and we get zero point nine nine nine… rather than one.
The missing amount is small, but a proof cannot quietly discard it.
We can handle that problem in two different ways.
Keep fractions exact… and when a value is not known exactly, keep a justified interval around it.
This is Part Two of Landau Windows ACL Two: exact arithmetic with imperfect information.
Our aim is to make every later numerical claim carry its own guarantee.
A fraction gives a number a finite description using integers.
For two thirds, record a numerator of two… and a denominator of three.
The denominator must be positive in the convention we will use.
Four sixths describes the same rational number, so different pairs can have the same meaning.
ACL2 reduces rational numbers to a canonical form; four sixths is read as two thirds.
Negative fractions also have finite descriptions: record a sign together with the numerator and denominator.
This does not add a new kind of infinite object to Peano Arithmetic.
Signed integers and fractions can be encoded using natural numbers, with arithmetic rules for their representations.
For example, comparing two thirds with three quarters becomes comparing two times four… with three times three.
Eight is less than nine, so two thirds is less than three quarters.
That is the sort of explicit arithmetic connection we need when we move between a convenient notation and a weaker foundation.
These examples illustrate that connection; they are not a full formal interpretation of all of ACL2.
Let us add one third and one sixth, slowly.
Split each third into two sixths… so one third becomes two sixths.
Now the denominators agree.
Two sixths plus one sixth gives three sixths… which is one half.
No decimal approximation was needed at any step.
In ACL2, the expression on screen asks for exactly that sum.
The slash inside a rational literal is part of its written number representation.
A slash at the start of a parenthesized expression is the division operation.
Both expressions here produce the same exact rational answer.
The small theorem below records this equality in our separately checked teaching book.
Exact arithmetic solves rounding in these operations, but it does not tell us every value we will later want to study.
For those, we need bounds.

chapter: An interval is a claim about a value

sentences.text: Suppose we know that x lies between one half and three quarters.
We draw the whole interval… and then place x somewhere inside it.
Two thirds is one possible example, but the guarantee should not depend on that particular choice.
Move the point and the claim remains true… as long as it stays between the endpoints.
The square brackets mean that both endpoints are allowed.
An interval is not a guess that its midpoint is correct.
It is a claim that the value is at least the lower endpoint… and at most the upper endpoint.
Making that claim requires evidence; drawing the picture does not supply it.
We will first assume input bounds are justified and prove that our arithmetic preserves them.
Later episodes explain how the project constructs bounds for its less elementary functions.
Here the endpoints and the values in the ACL2 statements are rational numbers.

chapter: Give the interval an actual ACL2 definition

sentences.text: We need an explicit representation before we name an interval function.
Store the lower and upper endpoints in a pair.
Cons builds that pair… car retrieves its first component… and cdr retrieves its second component.
The dot in this printed pair separates those two components.
It is a dotted pair, rather than the proper list of digits used in Part One.
The function lw-intervalp checks that a pair exists, that both endpoints are rational, and that the lower one does not exceed the upper one.
Here is the complete definition from the project's interval kernel, copied into our isolated teaching book.
Consp checks for a pair… rationalp checks each endpoint… and the last comparison checks their order.
Once we have read those checks, we can fold the definition into a compact name.
Now define the claim that the pair contains a value.
Lw-contains requires a valid interval, a rational value, and the two endpoint inequalities.
The conjunction and means that all those requirements must hold.
This is a test of a supplied interval and value; it does not discover an unknown value for us.
We will use its name as shorthand for that full claim.

chapter: Add lower to lower, upper to upper

sentences.text: Take x in the interval from one half to three quarters.
Take y in the interval from one quarter to one third.
We want bounds for x plus y that work for every allowed choice.
The smallest possible sum comes from adding the two lower endpoints.
One half plus one quarter is three quarters.
The largest possible sum comes from adding the two upper endpoints.
Three quarters plus one third is thirteen twelfths.
Here is lw-interval-add: cons stores the two sums, using car for lower endpoints and cdr for upper endpoints.
There is no search for the hidden values in this definition.
The reason it works is that inequalities can be added.
If each lower endpoint is below its value, their sum is below the sum of the values… and the upper endpoints give the other inequality.
The theorem lw-contains-add says exactly that the output interval contains x plus y whenever the two input intervals contain x and y.
The letters in the source are left-value and right-value; those play the roles of x and y in our picture.
That is a general statement about all rational inputs satisfying the hypotheses… not just the points we animated.
Subtraction needs more care.
Use the same two input intervals, but now consider x minus y.
Subtracting the two lower endpoints would give one quarter.
That cannot be a safe lower bound: choose x equal to one half… and y equal to one third.
Their difference is one sixth, which is smaller than one quarter.
To make x minus y as small as possible, make x small… and y large.
So the lower output is the lower endpoint of x minus the upper endpoint of y.
To make the difference large, make x large… and y small.
The upper output is the upper endpoint of x minus the lower endpoint of y.
Those choices give the interval from one sixth to one half.
The complete definition of lw-interval-sub shows the crossed components explicitly.
After folding it into its name, the theorem guarantees containment for every allowed rational x and y.
This crossing of endpoints is part of the mathematical guarantee, not a cosmetic choice in the code.

chapter: A negative scale reverses the order

sentences.text: Next multiply an interval by a fixed rational coefficient.
For a coefficient of two, every point moves to twice its original value.
The interval from one half to three quarters becomes the interval from one to three halves.
A negative coefficient introduces one more step.
Multiplication by minus two reflects the points across zero… as well as doubling their distance from zero.
The old lower endpoint now lands on the right, at minus one.
The old upper endpoint lands on the left, at minus three halves.
We must therefore reverse the endpoint order to store a valid interval.
Here is the full definition of lw-interval-scale.
The if expression chooses a branch according to the sign of the coefficient.
A nonnegative coefficient keeps the order… and a negative coefficient swaps which endpoint supplies the lower output.
Zero belongs to the first branch and collapses the interval to the single point zero.
The corresponding containment theorem includes the hypothesis that the coefficient is rational.
We have now justified addition, subtraction, and multiplication by a fixed rational number.

chapter: Keep width separate from error radius

sentences.text: How much uncertainty have we carried through the calculation?
The width of an interval is its upper endpoint minus its lower endpoint.
Our first interval has width one quarter… and our second has width one twelfth.
Their sum interval has width one third, the sum of those two widths.
Subtraction also adds the input widths, because its endpoints cross.
Multiplication by a fixed coefficient multiplies width by that coefficient's absolute value.
We should distinguish width from a symmetric error radius.
For an interval centered on an approximation, the radius is the distance from the center to either endpoint.
A symmetric interval's full width is twice that radius.
So a width of two hundredths means an error radius of one hundredth… when the displayed approximation is its midpoint.
The containment guarantee comes from the endpoints, whether or not we choose to display a midpoint.
Keeping these two quantities separate prevents a factor-of-two mistake in an error budget.

chapter: Build an error budget for a whole calculation

sentences.text: Consider the expression two times x minus y.
Suppose x is enclosed from ninety-nine hundredths to one hundred and one hundredths.
Suppose y is enclosed from one hundred and ninety-nine hundredths to two hundred and one hundredths.
Both input intervals have an error radius of one hundredth around their displayed centers.
Doubling x doubles its error radius… and subtracting y adds the other radius.
The total output radius is therefore three hundredths.
The resulting interval runs from minus three hundredths to plus three hundredths.
That interval crosses zero, so these bounds alone cannot establish a positive result.
Now suppose a more precise computation justifies narrower input intervals.
Enclose x from exactly one point zero zero one… to exactly one point zero zero three.
Enclose y from exactly one point nine nine nine… to exactly two point zero zero one.
These terminating decimals are exact fractions, and the narrower bounds still require a new justification.
The output now runs from one thousandth to seven thousandths.
Its midpoint is four thousandths and its error radius is three thousandths… so the entire interval is positive.
Every endpoint in this example is calculated by the functions we have already defined.
An error budget tells us how accurate the ingredients must be for the final claim we want.

chapter: A positive lower endpoint is a certificate

sentences.text: Let us isolate that final claim.
If an interval crosses zero, its midpoint might be positive while an allowed value is negative.
If its lower endpoint equals zero, the interval still permits zero.
A strictly positive lower endpoint rules out both possibilities.
Once x is at least that endpoint, x must be positive as well.
The ACL2 comparison on screen checks only the stored lower endpoint.
The theorem adds the essential hypothesis: the interval really contains the value.
Without that hypothesis, a positive pair of endpoints says nothing about an unrelated quantity.
This small implication turns a computed bound into a certificate of a mathematical inequality.
The same idea works above any rational threshold, by comparing the lower endpoint with that threshold.
The difficulty in a larger proof is to justify the enclosure and make it narrow enough.

chapter: A strict margin makes precision sufficient

sentences.text: There is a useful converse guarantee behind that last difficulty.
Suppose the true value is above a threshold by more than an error budget.
Also suppose our interval contains that value and has width at most that budget.
Then its lower endpoint must already lie above the threshold.
Here is a numerical picture: threshold zero… width budget one tenth… and value one fifth.
Any containing interval of width at most one tenth cannot stretch all the way down to zero.
To see the general reason, call the endpoints lower and upper.
The value is no larger than upper… so the distance from lower to the value is no greater than the full interval width.
That distance is at most the error budget.
Rearrange: lower is at least the value minus the budget.
And the assumed strict margin makes that last quantity greater than the threshold.
The theorem lw-lower-gt-of-margin states this guarantee for rational values, thresholds, and budgets.
We are not asking the program to look up an unknown true value.
The theorem says that when mathematics supplies a sufficient margin, any justified interval with the required precision must reveal it.
This is what will connect an error budget to a search that is guaranteed to succeed.

chapter: A rational certificate and its real meaning

sentences.text: One boundary still deserves attention.
The containment function we showed quantifies over rational values.
It does not quietly turn an irrational number into an ordinary ACL2 rational object.
Yet rational calculations can provide evidence for a bound on an irrational quantity.
For example, seven fifths squared is less than two… and three halves squared is greater than two.
Clear the positive denominators and these become the integer comparisons forty-nine is less than fifty… and eight is less than nine.
Our teaching book checks those exact arithmetic facts.
To conclude that the positive square root of two lies between seven fifths and three halves, we also use the mathematical meaning of a positive square root and the order of positive squares.
The integer certificate and its interpretation are related, but they are distinct proof obligations.
The project follows that discipline: arithmetic constructions in ACL2, and explicit interpretation statements connecting them to the classical quantities.
Peano Arithmetic can describe finite integer calculations; a complete reduction must also explain what its encoded statements mean.
We should track that bridge as carefully as the numerical operations themselves.

chapter: From one certified bound to a finite search

sentences.text: We began with a decimal display that silently changed one third.
Exact rational arithmetic removed that particular error.
Intervals then let us carry justified uncertainty through addition, subtraction, and scaling.
We kept width separate from radius, composed an error budget, and proved why a positive lower endpoint certifies positivity.
A strict mathematical margin tells us when enough precision must make that certificate appear.
These are small reusable guarantees, and the interval definitions come directly from this repository.
Next we will lay down a finite grid, examine its intervals, and return an address where a certified inequality holds.
Checking a returned address is only one obligation.
We must also prove that the search finds an address under the intended hypotheses.
That is where the exact bounds from this episode become part of the Landau construction.
